To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there are no differences in earnings or benefits for Black baccalaureate degree holders who attended HBCUs versus non HBCUs.
there are no differences in labor market outcomes between graduates of HBCU and non-HBCUs.
there are no statistically significant differences in the labor market outcomes between Black graduates of HSCUs and Black graduates of non-HBCUs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
whether the HBCU experience is a positive experience for Black college graduates in terms of the labor market.
the question: Are there significant differences in the earnings and benefits of baccalaureate degree holders from HBCUs versus non-HBCUs?
whether HBCUs are effective in producing Black graduates who are able to attain human capital and, in turn, labor market outcomes that are equivalent to non HBCU graduates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no statistically significant differences in earnings and benefits for Black college graduates of HBCU institutions compared to non-HBCUs.
there are no disadvantages to Black baccalaureate degree holders who graduate from HBCUs in the labor market.
HBCUs do not serve as a barrier to the acquisition of human capital for Black college students.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HBCUs serve an important role in the educational attainment of Blacks in the United States.
HBCUs do not disadvantage Black students in terms of labor outcomes and that the human capital theory framework is useful for explaining labor market outcomes for HBCU students.
Black students who attend HBCUs are no worse off than Black students who attend non HBCUs in regards to labor market outcomes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Black students who attend HBCUs are not at a disadvantage when compared to their Black counterparts at predominantly White institutions (PWIs).
the labor market outcomes for Black baccalaureate degree holders from HBCUs are not worse than those from non-HBCUs.
HBCUs are not a liability for Black students in terms of human capital development and subsequent labor market outcomes.
